title: Abstraction
starter: Sketch a map that would get a new pupil from the school gate to your classroom. What did you leave out, and why?
starterAnswer: Accept any sensible attempt: this is a hook, not an assessment.
Look for the vocabulary from the lesson objectives appearing in students' own words.
Students who are stuck should still write something: the experience will correct it.
starterNote: Take two or three answers, then leave it open. Come back to it in the plenary, when they can answer it properly.

stations.name: Computational thinking
facts: Computational thinking is how you approach a problem so a computer can solve it.
It has three parts: abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking.
They are used together, not one after the other.
stations.challenge: Name the three parts of computational thinking and write one line on each.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Computational thinking is how you approach a problem so a computer can solve it.
Also credit: It has three parts: abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking.

questions.q: What are the three parts of computational thinking?
Which part of computational thinking is each activity?
questions.a: Deciding a train timetable only needs times and stations = Abstraction; Ignoring the colour of a car in a traffic simulation = Abstraction; Splitting a game into scoring, drawing and input = Decomposition; Listing the smaller problems inside a big one = Decomposition; Writing the steps to find the largest number = Algorithmic thinking; Working out the order the checks must happen in = Algorithmic thinking

stations.name: What abstraction is
facts: Abstraction means removing detail that does not matter to the problem.
What is left is a model: simpler than reality, and good enough to work with.
What counts as unnecessary depends entirely on the problem you are solving.
stations.challenge: Write your own definition of abstraction, with an example that is not a map.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Abstraction means removing detail that does not matter to the problem.
Also credit: What is left is a model: simpler than reality, and good enough to work with.

questions.q: What does abstraction mean in computational thinking?
questions.a: Removing detail that is not needed to solve the problem

questions.q: Why is what counts as 'unnecessary' not fixed?
questions.a: It depends on the problem: a detail that matters in one model is noise in another

stations.name: A worked example
facts: A school register needs a name, a form group and present or absent.
It does not need eye colour, shoe size or favourite subject.
Adding unnecessary data makes the system slower, larger and harder to keep correct.
stations.challenge: List four things a school register stores and three it deliberately does not.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A school register needs a name, a form group and present or absent.
Also credit: It does not need eye colour, shoe size or favourite subject.

questions.q: Which details does a school register need? Select all that apply.
questions.a: The pupil's name; The date; Whether they are present; Which form group they are in

questions.q: Why is storing unnecessary data a problem?
questions.a: It takes more space, slows the system and gives more to keep accurate and secure

stations.name: Models of the world
facts: A weather forecast is a model: it keeps pressure and temperature, and ignores individual raindrops.
A satnav keeps roads, junctions and speeds, and ignores what the buildings look like.
Every model is wrong in some way. A useful model is wrong about things that don't matter.
stations.challenge: Choose a program you use and say what it deliberately ignores about the real world.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A weather forecast is a model: it keeps pressure and temperature, and ignores individual raindrops.
Also credit: A satnav keeps roads, junctions and speeds, and ignores what the buildings look like.

questions.q: For a satnav, is each detail necessary or unnecessary?
questions.a: The speed limit on a road = Necessary; Which roads connect to which = Necessary; Whether a road is one way = Necessary; The colour of the houses = Unnecessary; How many trees line the road = Unnecessary; The name of the road's builder = Unnecessary

questions.q: A flight simulator ignores the weight of the paint on the aircraft. Why is that acceptable?
questions.a: It is far too small to change the behaviour being modelled

stations.name: Abstraction in programs
facts: A variable name like score is an abstraction: it hides which memory address holds the value.
A subprogram is an abstraction: you call it without needing to know how it works inside.
Layers of abstraction let one person work on a game without understanding the graphics card.
stations.challenge: Explain how calling a subprogram is an example of abstraction.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: A variable name like score is an abstraction: it hides which memory address holds the value.
Also credit: A subprogram is an abstraction: you call it without needing to know how it works inside.

questions.q: How is a subprogram an example of abstraction?
questions.a: You use it by name without needing to know how it works inside

questions.q: Why do layers of abstraction matter in a large project?
questions.a: Each person can work on their layer without understanding all the others

stations.name: Answering abstraction questions
facts: Say what is kept and what is removed, and why each decision was made.
Link the decision to the purpose of the system.
One mark is usually for an example, so always give one.
stations.challenge: Plan a four-mark answer on abstraction in a bus timetable app.
challengeAnswer: Model answer: Say what is kept and what is removed, and why each decision was made.
Also credit: Link the decision to the purpose of the system.

questions.q: Which is the strongest exam answer about a library system?
questions.a: It stores the title, author and whether a book is on loan, but not the paper weight, because that never affects lending

questions.q: A question asks how abstraction has been used in an underground map. What earns the marks?
questions.a: Naming what was removed, such as true distances and surface geography, and why that helps a passenger

final.name: Final challenge: keep or cut

questions.q: For a cycle hire app, is each detail necessary or unnecessary?
questions.a: Where each docking station is = Necessary; How many bikes are free at each station = Necessary; Whether a route has a cycle lane = Necessary; The gradient of a hill = Necessary; The make of each bike's bell = Unnecessary; The name of the street's architect = Unnecessary; What colour the docking station is painted = Unnecessary; Which shops are on the route = Unnecessary

final.note: Students should have predicted these on the worksheet before tapping the star. Mark the prediction, not just the final answer.

exam.q: State what is meant by abstraction.
points: It has three parts: abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking.
Abstraction means removing detail that does not matter to the problem.
Layers of abstraction let one person work on a game without understanding the graphics card.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: Give two examples of abstraction in a computer system.
points: Computational thinking is how you approach a problem so a computer can solve it.
It has three parts: abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking.
Abstraction means removing detail that does not matter to the problem.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 2.

exam.q: A company is writing a program to plan delivery routes. Explain how abstraction would be used, giving examples of detail kept and removed.
points: Abstraction means removing detail that does not matter to the problem.
It has three parts: abstraction, decomposition and algorithmic thinking.
They are used together, not one after the other.
Layers of abstraction let one person work on a game without understanding the graphics card.
Say what is kept and what is removed, and why each decision was made.
Accept any other correct point relevant to the question.
exam.note: One mark per point, to a maximum of 6.

common: Naming a term without saying what it does: most questions need the term and its purpose.
Answering 'it's faster' or 'it's better' with no reason: link it to the characteristic the question is about.
Repeating the question in the answer and stopping there.
